title: Human Centric School Lighting Evidence based design of light characters and automatic light variation, for a classroom in Malmö
research_question: To develop design principles for dynamic Human Centric School Lighting that enables appropriate variation of light intensity and color temperature, and to suggest a set of light characters clarifying different lighting needs in a classroom.

participants.description: Pupils (7th grade, age 12-16 years) and teachers in a classroom in Malmö, Sweden (N=23 pupils for Case Study 1 & 2, N=5 for interviews). A comparative study included pupils (age 7-13 years, N=20) and teachers (N=4) in Kongsberg, Norway.
participants.recruitment: Malmö City expressed interest in testing Human Centric School Lighting and helped with contacts for a classroom installation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A classroom in Malmö, Sweden, equipped with 12 Candelux 60x60 LED panels (3000 K to 6000 K, CRI 85, 3800 lm) and a control system for automatic light variation and manual selection of light characters. The study involved two rounds of installations and evaluations. Light characters included 'Activating' (700/500 lux, 6500 K), 'Calming/Dialogue' (350/500 lux, 2700 K), 'Smartboard' (dimmed front, light in back), 'Neutral' (500 lux, 4000 K), 'Presentation' (brighter front, dimmer back). Automatic variation schemes adjusted intensity and CCT throughout the day.

A classroom in Kongsberg, Norway, with Glamox Luxo Modul R 600 LED Premium luminaires (Ra > 90, tuneable white) controlled by KNX to DALI. Settings included 'Morning level of the awakening light' (650 lux, 6500 K), 'Awakening light' (1000 lux, 6500 K), 'Neutral light' (300 lux, 3500 K), and 'Restful light' (300 lux, 2700 K).

mechanisms: Blue light influences circadian cycles via intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) and melatonin regulation.
Short-wavelength light blocks melatonin production, promoting wakefulness.
Red light has acute alerting effects through brain activity without suppressing melatonin.
Lower light intensity can reduce voice levels.
Higher color temperature (4000 K) can increase concentration.
Light in the 460–500 nm range has an activating effect.
Warm light has a calming effect.
Redder light provides good conditions for dialogues by enhancing facial color nuances (oxygenated/not oxygenated blood), aiding interpretation of emotional states.
Sudden, unexpected light changes cause prediction error and distraction.
Even light distribution can lead to a 'lifeless' atmosphere due to lack of dramatic contrast and poor visualization of facial mimics.
Overstimulation from intense blue light can cause headaches, especially in sensitive individuals.
Teachers use specific light settings as pedagogical tools to signal activity changes (e.g., 'time to concentrate').
The new recessed LED fittings create an 'open' impression by appearing as openings through the roof.
implementation_implications: Automatic light variation is needed to prevent static light settings and associated negative effects (e.g., headaches from prolonged activating light).
Automatic light variation should include intense blue light in the morning for awakening and better sleep, and red light in the afternoon for concentration without affecting sleep.
Manually controlled light scenes should include 'Activating light' for high concentration tasks and a 'Dialogue' mode with warm light.
Exposure to intense blue light should be limited in duration and intensity, especially in manual 'Activation' mode.
Light transitions should be slow and unnoticeable to avoid distraction, but shorter transitions can be effective as a pedagogical tool.
The classroom light should start with a color temperature similar to the corridor to avoid sharp transitions.
Light character names should be clear and intuitive for teachers (e.g., rename 'Calming light').
A 'Presentation' mode (more light at the front, less at the back) should be introduced.
The use of white light (4000 K) at lower intensity should be increased.
Different layers of light (e.g., spotlights) should be added to create a more dynamic and less lifeless atmosphere.
Wall washers in the front of the classroom could provide more horizontal light into pupils' eyes.
Environments should offer restorative properties, not just high-pitched stimuli.
Multiple layers of light and control of reflectance/distribution (e.g., dark furniture in corners) can support sensitive individuals.
Light variation design should be simple, scientifically proven, and user-adapted with an easy-to-use interface.
Teachers need knowledge about the control system and how light properties affect users.
A common language for new lighting properties is needed to improve communication between designers, producers, installers, and programmers.
Iterative design processes with preliminary evaluations are preferable for good design results.
Demonstrations and experimental installations are crucial for mobilizing new technical potential and scientific knowledge in Human Centric Lighting.

limitations: Limited knowledge exists on how to tailor light variation patterns to individual needs, time of day, and activities.
Technical delays and commissioning issues prevented the initially planned case study of a finalized installation.
The thesis primarily focuses on temporal light variation, with limited attention to spatial light variations.
No daylight-related control of lighting levels was included due to practical and economic reasons.
The thesis does not aim to contribute to basic scientific knowledge on non-visual effects influencing circadian cycles.
The study did not include new furniture or plants, which could enhance the overall effect.
It is difficult to find a measurement method that accurately describes the total experience of dynamic light environments, leaving room for misrepresentation in sales.
The automatic light variation was more complicated to install than expected and its functionality could not be fully verified as specified.
Technical start-up problems led to a significant dip in illuminance during the first minute of some light character activations.
Strange and irregular light variations (e.g., 400 Hz with 86% peak-to-peak variation) were observed on the oscilloscope screen, indicating potential flicker issues.
